appraisal_events.evidence: « Swann comme beaucoup de gens avait l'esprit paresseux et manquait d'invention » ; son amour de la sincérité « n'étant pas désintéressé, ne l'avait pas rendu meilleur » ; il l'aimait « comme une proxénète pouvant le tenir au courant de la vie de sa maîtresse » ; « En somme il mentait autant qu'Odette parce que, plus malheureux qu'elle, il n'était pas moins égoïste. » Il finit par « regarder mourir leur amour ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator, in his own voice rather than through Swann's, convicts Swann of mental laziness, self-interested lying and egoism, and stages the collapse of his ability to judge anyone at all after the anonymous letter. The wish for Odette's death, the Mahomet II identification and the dying love close the movement as sustained diminishment.

appraisal_events.evidence: La lettre anonyme dit « qu'Odette avait été la maîtresse d'innombrables hommes (dont on lui citait quelques-uns parmi lesquels Forcheville, M. de Bréauté et le peintre), de femmes, et qu'elle fréquentait les maisons de passe » ; puis le souvenir de Mme Verdurin (« je saurai bien te dégeler, tu n'es pas de marbre ») rejoint « sa conversation de mauvais goût », ces plaisanteries « lui faisaient perdre de son innocence ».
appraisal_events.explanation: An anonymous denunciation attaches Odette to a chain of named lovers and to disreputable milieux; Swann first dismisses it, but the narrator has just discredited the grounds of that dismissal, and the closing Filles de Marbre sequence lets the accusation regain force. Her local standing sinks without the narrator confirming the charges.

status_effects.explanation: The narrator's explicit verdicts — lazy-minded, uninventive, as much a liar as Odette, no less egoistic, not made better by his love of truth — lower Swann sharply within the passage.
He has lost all hope of being loved, cannot bring himself to question or even kiss Odette, is displaced by Forcheville's Egypt trip, and ends sitting apart watching their love die.

The letter and the reactivated Mme Verdurin memory strip her of the innocence Swann had lent her, and the narrator himself notes that she lies; the charges remain unverified, so the movement is somewhat rather than clearly diminishing.

ambiguities: The passage neither confirms nor refutes the anonymous letter's accusations against Odette: it dismantles Swann's grounds for rejecting them (mental laziness, projection of the known onto the unknown) and lets the Mme Verdurin memory revive the sapphic suspicion, but the narrator never speaks to their truth. Read as endorsed, E2 would justify a -2 for Odette; read as pure jealous construction, it would justify 0.

The suspect named « Lorédan » (« D'abord Lorédan avait des raisons d'en vouloir à Odette ») is treated here as the coachman Rémi named in the immediately preceding sentence; the reference sheet does not list that surface form, and if the two are distinct men the suspicion catalogue includes an unlisted servant.
